title: Al-Baqarah: The Cow
intro: 26 days through Al-Baqarah, the longest surah of the Quran, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Al-Baqarah, "The Cow", is the second and longest surah of the Quran: 286 verses, revealed in Medina after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ moved there. It opens with the letters Alif, Lam, Mim, then this verse. "Those who ward off (evil)" is Pickthall's phrase for the muttaqin, people of taqwa, a mindful awareness of Allah.

After describing believers, disbelievers and hypocrites, the surah turns to address everyone at once: "O mankind!" It is the first time the Quran, in its written order, calls out to all of humanity this way. The call rests on creation itself: the One who made you and those before you.

A whole life in one verse. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir explain "ye were dead" as the time before a person existed: then comes life, then death, then life again at the resurrection, and finally the return to Allah. The question invites reflection on the One who gave life in the first place.

Allah has told the angels He will place a khalifah, a vicegerent, on earth. He then teaches the Prophet Adam "all the names", which commentators understand as the names of things, and asks the angels to name them. This is their humble reply. Some Muslims recite it before studying, as a reminder of where knowledge comes from.

Allah commands the angels to bow before Adam, a prostration that classical commentators describe as one of honour, not worship. All obey except Iblis, who refuses out of pride. Elsewhere the Quran says he was one of the jinn, and two verses later it calls him Satan. "Demurred" here means refused.

After Adam and his wife eat from the forbidden tree, Adam receives "words" from his Lord, repents, and is forgiven. Many commentators identify these words with the prayer in Al-A'raf 7:23: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves." In Islamic teaching the slip is forgiven, and it is not passed on to Adam's children.

This is the story that gives the surah its name. The Prophet Musa (Moses) tells his people to sacrifice a cow, and instead of simply doing it they answer with questions: what age, what colour, what kind. Each answer narrows the task, until "they sacrificed her, though almost they did not."

Two pillars of Islam appear together here: "worship", Pickthall's word for salah, the ritual prayer, and "the poor-due", zakat, the obligatory alms. The Quran pairs the two many times. The verse adds that any good a person sends ahead is waiting with Allah.

"Countenance" translates wajh, literally "face". Some classical commentators link this verse to voluntary prayer while travelling, or praying when the direction is unclear, as well as to the later change of the qiblah. Its wider point is that East and West alike belong to Allah, who can be turned to from anywhere. "All-Embracing" is al-Wasi'.

"Be! and it is" renders kun fa-yakun, a phrase that returns several times in the Quran to describe Allah's creative command. "Originator" translates Badi', one who brings something into being with no earlier model. In the Quran's picture, creation needs only His word.

The surah turns to the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), the model of faith. "Surrender" and "I have surrendered" translate aslim and aslamtu, from the same root as the words Islam and Muslim. The next verse describes him passing this same surrender on to his sons, as did the Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob).

This verse sits in the passage about the change of qiblah, the direction of prayer, from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca, early in the Medinan years. Rather than dwell on directions, it points to what matters: racing one another in good deeds. The Arabic, fastabiqu al-khayrat, is often quoted on its own.

One of the Quran's most intimate promises: remember Allah, and He will remember you. Remembrance, dhikr, covers prayer, recitation and the simple repetition of Allah's names and praises. Pickthall's "reject not Me" renders a word that also means "do not be ungrateful to Me".

Sabr, translated here as "steadfastness", means patient endurance: holding firm in difficulty, keeping up good deeds, and holding back from wrong. This verse pairs it with prayer as the two sources of help. It opens a short passage about trials and loss.

The verse before warns of trials: fear, hunger, and loss of wealth, lives and crops, with good news for the steadfast. This verse gives their response, inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, which Muslims say on hearing of a death and in moments of loss, large or small.

A one-line statement of tawhid, the oneness of Allah, the foundation of Islamic belief. It ends with the same two names of mercy that open the Bismillah. The next verse points to the evidence in creation: the heavens and the earth, night and day, ships, rain, winds and clouds.

This comes in the passage on the Hajj pilgrimage: after the rites, some ask only for good in this world, while others ask for good in both. According to a hadith reported by Anas ibn Malik, this was the supplication the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ made most often. It remains one of the best-known prayers in Islam.

This verse appears, perhaps surprisingly, in the middle of a long passage on marriage and divorce. Scholars have long differed over "the midmost prayer": many hold that it is the afternoon prayer, Asr, while others name a different one. "With devotion" renders qanitin, standing in humble obedience.

posts.display: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Unto Him belongeth whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is in the earth.
posts.display_original: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
posts.caption: The opening of Ayat al-Kursi, the Verse of the Throne, too long to show in full. In a hadith recorded in Sahih Muslim it is called the greatest verse in the Book of Allah. Al-Hayy al-Qayyum, "the Alive, the Eternal", names the One who lives forever and sustains all things. Many Muslims recite the whole verse after prayers and before sleep.

Right after Ayat al-Kursi comes one of the Quran's most quoted lines. Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir explain that since the truth has been made clear, there is no need to force anyone into faith. "False deities" renders taghut, anything worshipped in place of Allah, and the "firm handhold" is al-urwa al-wuthqa.

The surah's long passage on charity opens with this image: one grain grows seven ears with a hundred grains in each, seven hundred from one. "In Allah's way" (fi sabil Allah) means giving for the sake of Allah. The verse adds that Allah multiplies it further still for whom He wills.

The verses around this one warn against spoiling charity by reminding people of it or hurting their feelings. A kind word and forgiveness, it says, are worth more than a gift that wounds. "Absolute" renders al-Ghani, the One free of all need, and "Clement" al-Halim, the Forbearing.

Hikmah, wisdom, is described here as a gift from Allah, and whoever receives it has received "abundant good". Elsewhere the Quran often pairs wisdom with the Scripture as something the prophets teach. "Men of understanding" renders ulu al-albab, people of insight.

Al-Baqarah forbids riba, usury, in the verses just before this one. Then it turns to the borrower who cannot pay: the verse grants time until things ease, and calls cancelling the debt as charity better still. It is a window onto the Quran's concern for people in financial hardship.

Early authorities named different verses as the last to be revealed; Ibn Abbas is reported to have said it was this one. It lifts the eye from the details of trade and debt to the day when every soul is repaid in full. The very next verse, about writing down loans, is the longest in the Quran.

posts.display: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope. For it (is only) that which it hath earned, and against it (only) that which it hath deserved. Our Lord! Condemn us not if we forget, or miss the mark!
posts.display_original: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ رَبَّنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذْنَآ إِن نَّسِينَآ أَوْ أَخْطَأْنَا
posts.caption: The final verse of Al-Baqarah, shown in part. It opens with the promise that no soul is burdened beyond its capacity, then becomes a prayer for pardon, mercy and help. According to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the last two verses of this surah are enough for whoever recites them at night. Thank you for reading Al-Baqarah with us.
